meta.scoring: For each statement: value = (answer - 3) * direction. direction +1 means agreeing pushes toward poleB, -1 means agreeing pushes toward poleA. Axis score = average of values (range -2 to +2), then multiply by 50 to get -100 (fully poleA) to +100 (fully poleB).
meta.notes: Question bank: 22 statements per axis (11 agree-direction, 11 disagree-direction) and 20 scenarios. Quick draws 1 agree-direction and 1 disagree-direction statement per axis (20 questions). Standard draws 3 and 3 per axis plus 8 scenarios (68 questions). Deep uses every statement and scenario (240 questions). Every quiz ends with a random 20 of the 40 history questions. Never reorder or delete existing statements or scenarios without bumping the answer-code version, and keep statement ids stable because the contradiction rules refer to them.

statements.text: Removing fuel subsidies is necessary even if it causes hardship in the short term.
Government should keep ownership of key sectors such as power, refineries and railways.
Privatising loss-making state enterprises usually makes them work better.
Government should set price controls on essentials like food and transport.
Lower taxes on businesses will create more jobs than government spending programmes.
The state should be the main creator of jobs for young people.
Competition between private companies lowers prices better than government regulation does.
Essential services such as water and electricity should be run by the state, not for profit.
Government should reduce its role in business so that entrepreneurs can grow faster.
The state should protect workers' wages and jobs even if businesses complain about the cost.
Young Nigerians are better served by starting private businesses than by waiting for government jobs.
Profits from natural resources should mostly go to public services and not to private companies.
The naira should be left to find its own value in the market, even when that makes imports more expensive.
Private universities, hospitals and power companies should be free to compete with public ones.
Government should sell its shares in companies it does not need to run.
Lower taxes on small businesses help ordinary people more than extra government spending does.
A person who builds a profitable business does more for the public than a government programme of the same size.
Government should run a national food reserve and guarantee minimum prices to farmers.
Strategic industries such as steel and fertiliser should be built and owned by the state.
Public spending on housing and healthcare should rise even if taxes have to rise too.
Basic healthcare should be provided by the state and not left to private firms.
Very large private companies should face tighter regulation, or be broken up, when they become too powerful.
States should control the natural resources found within their borders and pay tax to the centre.
Security is best handled by a single national police force.
Each state should be allowed to run its own police.
The federal government should set uniform standards for education and health across all states.
Nigeria needs a new constitution that shifts more power to the regions.
Too much devolution would weaken national unity.
State governments know their people's needs better than the federal government does.
A strong federal government is needed to keep the country together.
States should be free to set their own tax rates and keep most of what they collect.
Revenue from oil and gas should be shared by the federal government among all states.
Local governments should receive their funds directly and not through state governments.
The federal government should be able to take over a state's security in an emergency.
Each state should be free to decide how its own local governments are organised.
Groups of neighbouring states should be able to set up regional development bodies with their own budgets.
Federal agencies should not operate in matters the constitution leaves to the states.
Land in each state should be governed by that state's own laws and not by one national land law.
Each state should be able to set its own minimum wage.
One national school curriculum is better than each state setting its own.
Federal courts should be able to overrule state laws that conflict with national standards.
Major infrastructure such as ports, airports and railways should stay under federal control.
State elections should be run by the national electoral commission and not by state commissions.
Richer states should be required to help fund poorer ones through the federal budget.
Government should stay out of religious matters entirely.
Religious values should guide how laws are made.
State funding of religious pilgrimages should end.
Religious leaders should have a formal advisory role in government.
Religious education should be part of the public school curriculum.
A candidate's faith should play no part in how I vote.
Government should give public support to faith-based schools, hospitals and charities.
Laws should be made on reason and evidence, not religious teaching.
Prayers and religious observances have a proper place at official state events.
Religion is a private matter and should stay out of politics.
A leader's moral and religious character matters as much as his or her policies.
Public money should not be used to build or maintain places of worship.
Government should consult religious leaders before passing laws on family life and morals.
Public broadcasters should give regular airtime to religious programmes.
A leader who prays openly gives people more confidence in government.
Religious courts should be allowed to settle personal-law cases for people who choose them.
Public schools should begin the day with a prayer.
Politicians should not use religious language in their campaigns.
Government appointments should never take a candidate's religion into account.
Religious organisations should pay tax on their commercial activities.
Laws should apply in the same way to everyone, whatever their faith teaches.
Religious leaders should not endorse political candidates from the pulpit.
I feel more connected to my ethnic group than to Nigeria as a whole.
Nigeria's diversity is best managed through a strong shared national identity.
States should give priority in jobs and services to indigenes over residents from other states.
Ethnic-based political and cultural groups do more harm than good.
Groups that feel marginalised have a legitimate right to seek self-determination.
Every Nigerian should have exactly the same rights in every state, regardless of origin.
Nigerians should be proud of being Nigerian before being proud of their tribe.
My first loyalty is to my own people and community.
Schools should teach a shared national history that all Nigerians learn.
Each ethnic group should be able to govern its own affairs with little interference.
People should be able to hold public office in any state, whatever their origin.
Communities should have a say in who is allowed to settle and own land among them.
Friendships and marriages across ethnic lines make Nigeria stronger.
National youth service should continue because it mixes young people from different parts of the country.
A person should be able to claim the place where they were born and raised, whatever their parents' origin.
Official forms should not ask for a person's state of origin or ethnic group.
Nigerians should speak up when any group is mistreated, even if it is not their own.
Mother-tongue languages should be the main language of teaching in primary schools.
Traditional rulers should have a formal role in governing their communities.
People from my region should look out for each other first in business and politics.
Each ethnic group should have its own guaranteed voice in the national assembly, whatever its population.
It is natural to trust people from my own community more than strangers.
The presidency should rotate between the North and the South.
Appointments should be based on competence, regardless of state of origin.
The Federal Character principle is necessary to prevent exclusion.
Admission to universities and the civil service should use one merit standard nationwide.
Party tickets should balance region and religion.
Merit alone should decide who leads, even if one region ends up dominating.
Qualifications and track record should decide who gets government jobs and contracts.
Every region should have a guaranteed share of ministerial positions.
Quotas for states in federal institutions should be phased out over time.
Power sharing between regions matters more than choosing the most skilled leader.
A president from any region is acceptable if he or she is the best candidate.
Admission and hiring rules should give extra weight to under-represented regions.
Political parties should choose their candidates through open primaries and not through deals between zones.
Ministers should be tested on their qualifications before they are confirmed.
Public contracts should go to the firm with the best bid, whatever the owner's origin.
Judges should be promoted on performance and not on where they come from.
A person's state of origin should not appear on job applications.
Each geopolitical zone should hold the vice-presidency in turn.
State governors should reserve commissioner posts for each local government area.
Rotating the top offices keeps the peace better than always choosing the most able candidate.
Federal appointments should reflect the population share of each region.
Minority groups should be guaranteed a seat at the table even if they lose elections.
Armed groups should be defeated militarily before any negotiation.
Amnesty and rehabilitation programmes are effective ways to end insurgency.
Poverty and lack of opportunity are the main drivers of banditry.
Harsh punishment deters crime better than rehabilitation.
Community dialogue between farmers and herders will do more than military deployment.
The military budget should grow even if other sectors get less.
Negotiation with armed groups can save more lives than fighting them.
Criminals and armed groups understand only strength.
Investing in education and jobs in troubled regions is the best way to reduce violence.
The army should be given more freedom to act against armed groups.
Local community leaders should help design security responses.
Curfews and a heavy military presence are the best response to unrest.
Respected community and religious leaders can stop violence through mediation before it spreads.
Giving young people skills and jobs costs less than fighting them as criminals later.
Security forces should be trained to de-escalate before they use weapons.
Fair rules on land and water would reduce farmer-herder violence more than extra troops would.
People who leave armed groups should be given a path back into society.
Checkpoints and stop-and-search should be widespread in troubled areas.
Paying ransom or negotiating with kidnappers only encourages more kidnapping.
The state should strike first against groups that are planning violence.
A bigger army and police force is the first step towards peace.
Villages that knowingly host armed groups should face tough penalties.
Laws restricting same-sex relationships are appropriate.
The death penalty should be abolished.
Cannabis should be decriminalised for medical use.
Women should have equal inheritance and land rights under law, even where custom says otherwise.
The law should protect the traditional family structure over changing social norms.
Government should regulate public dress and morality standards.
Individuals should be free to make their own choices about marriage and family, within the law.
Society is stronger when traditional gender roles are respected.
Freedom of expression should be protected even when speech offends traditional values.
Schools and media should promote traditional moral values.
Sex education should be taught in secondary schools.
Divorce and having children outside marriage should be discouraged by society.
Adults should be free to decide how to dress in public, within the law.
Women should be as free as men to hold any job or office.
Couples should be free to live together before marriage without social disapproval.
Nigerian films, music and art should be free from government censorship.
Local customs should give way when they conflict with an individual's legal rights.
Respect for elders should guide how families and communities make decisions.
Tradition and custom are a better guide to right and wrong than modern ideas.
Parents, not schools, should decide what children learn about sex and relationships.
Bride price and other marriage customs should be protected by law.
Public entertainment should follow community standards of decency.
Nigeria needs a strong leader more than it needs strong institutions.
Courts should be able to overturn executive decisions even when those decisions are popular.
Term limits should be strictly enforced for every elected office.
Military rule can be better than a failing democracy.
The electoral commission should be fully independent of the president's appointment.
Criticism of government should sometimes be restricted for the sake of national stability.
No official, including the president, should be above the law.
Sometimes democracy is too slow and a firm hand gets things done faster.
An independent press and civil society are essential for good government.
A president should be able to override parliament in a crisis.
Election disputes should be settled by courts and independent bodies, not by politicians.
Protests that disrupt public order should be firmly restricted.
The legislature should be able to investigate and question the president.
Local government elections should be held on time, every time, by an independent body.
Judges should be appointed through an open process with public input.
Citizens should be free to take the government to court over its decisions.
Political parties should choose their leaders through internal elections that outsiders can observe.
A leader who gets results should be allowed to stay in office longer than the law allows.
Too many checks on the executive make it hard to get things done.
In an emergency the president should be able to rule by decree.
Security services should be free to detain suspects without trial when national security is at stake.
One dominant party brings more stability than competition between many parties.
Nigeria should restrict imports to protect local producers.
Foreign investment should be welcomed with few restrictions.
Nigeria should deepen ECOWAS integration, including free movement of people.
Foreign ownership of key industries should be limited.
Nigeria should sign international trade agreements even if some local industries suffer.
Foreign loans and aid come with too many conditions and should be reduced.
Nigerian companies benefit from competing with foreign companies.
Nigeria should prioritise buying Nigerian-made goods, even if they cost more.
Nigerians abroad should be encouraged to invest and bring back skills, with few restrictions.
Foreign influence in Nigerian politics and media should be tightly limited.
Nigeria should work closely with other African countries and global partners on trade.
Nigeria should depend less on international institutions and foreign advice.
Nigerian students and workers gain a lot from studying and working abroad.
Foreign professionals should be able to work in Nigeria without many hurdles.
Nigeria should join regional trade blocs even if it gives up some control over its own tariffs.
International courts and bodies are a fair way to settle disputes between countries.
Foreign media and entertainment should be freely available to Nigerian audiences.
Nigeria should build its own cars, phones and machines even if it takes a long time.
Foreign companies should be required to hire mostly Nigerians and use Nigerian suppliers.
Nigeria should avoid borrowing from foreign lenders.
Natural resources should be developed mainly by Nigerian companies.
Nigeria should put its own interests first, even when this upsets trading partners.
Corrupt officials should face very long jail terms and full asset seizure.
Digitising government services does more against corruption than prosecutions.
Better public-sector pay and transparency will reduce corruption more than harsher punishment.
Convicted officials should be barred from politics for life.
Plea deals in exchange for returning stolen funds are acceptable.
Anti-corruption agencies need broader powers of arrest and seizure.
Clear rules and open government data prevent more corruption than prisons do.
Fear of severe punishment is the main thing that stops officials from stealing.
Protecting whistleblowers is more effective than harsher penalties.
Corrupt officials should be publicly named and shamed after conviction.
Independent audits and open contracts are better tools than special courts.
Special courts with fast trials are needed to deal with corruption cases.
Putting budgets and contracts online will do more against corruption than building new prisons.
Government should pay civil servants well enough that they have no need to take bribes.
Automating approvals and rotating officials reduces corruption better than arrests do.
Reporting corruption should be easy and safe for ordinary citizens.
Strict, public rules on how parties are funded would reduce the pressure to steal.
Public officials should have to explain the source of their wealth, with jail for those who cannot.
No one convicted of stealing public money should be allowed to keep any of it through a deal.
Corruption investigators should be free to arrest powerful people without waiting for political approval.
The assets of officials' close relatives should also be checked.
The worst cases of stealing public money deserve life sentences.

history.note: Factual questions only. Scored separately from the axes. Avoid adding questions that ask for blame or interpretation.

questions.question: In which year were the Northern and Southern Protectorates amalgamated?
questions.explanation: Lord Lugard oversaw the amalgamation in 1914.

questions.question: In which year did Nigeria gain independence?
questions.explanation: Independence was on 1 October 1960.

questions.question: In which year did Nigeria become a republic, with Nnamdi Azikiwe as its first president?
questions.explanation: Nigeria became a republic in 1963.

questions.question: Who was Nigeria's first Prime Minister?
questions.explanation: Tafawa Balewa led the government at independence.

questions.question: In which year did Nigeria's first military coup take place?
questions.explanation: The first coup was in January 1966.

questions.question: During which years was the Nigerian Civil War fought?
questions.explanation: The war ran from 1967 to 1970.

questions.question: Who declared the Republic of Biafra in 1967?
questions.explanation: Ojukwu declared Biafra's secession on 30 May 1967.

questions.question: The Land Use Act, which vests land in each state's governor, was introduced in which year?
questions.explanation: It was decreed in 1978 and later entrenched in the constitution.

questions.question: In which year did the capital officially move from Lagos to Abuja?
questions.explanation: The move was made official in December 1991.

questions.question: The Structural Adjustment Programme (SAP) was introduced under which leader?
questions.explanation: SAP began in 1986 under Babangida.

questions.question: Which election, widely believed to have been won by M.K.O. Abiola, was annulled in 1993?
questions.explanation: The June 12, 1993 election was annulled by the Babangida government.

questions.question: Who was executed in 1995 alongside eight other Ogoni activists?
questions.explanation: Ken Saro-Wiwa was executed in November 1995 under the Abacha regime.

questions.question: On what date did Nigeria return to civilian rule under the current Fourth Republic?
questions.explanation: Olusegun Obasanjo was sworn in on 29 May 1999.

questions.question: Which state was the first to reintroduce a full sharia criminal code around 1999-2000?
questions.explanation: Zamfara led the move, and several northern states followed.

questions.question: The 'Occupy Nigeria' protests of January 2012 were mainly a response to what?
questions.explanation: They followed the removal of the petrol subsidy under President Jonathan.

questions.question: In which year were the Chibok schoolgirls abducted?
questions.explanation: The abduction took place in April 2014.

questions.question: In 2015, who became the first opposition candidate to defeat a sitting Nigerian president at the polls?
questions.explanation: Buhari defeated Goodluck Jonathan.

questions.question: The #EndSARS protests, which peaked at Lekki Toll Gate, happened in which year?
questions.explanation: The protests peaked in October 2020.

questions.question: How many states does Nigeria have (not counting the FCT)?
questions.explanation: Nigeria has 36 states plus the Federal Capital Territory.

questions.question: The 1929 Aba Women's War was mainly a protest against what?
options: Land seizure by the Niger Company
questions.explanation: Women in southeastern Nigeria protested rumoured taxation and the warrant chief system.

questions.question: Who became Nigeria's Head of State after the January 1966 coup?
questions.explanation: Major General Aguiyi-Ironsi took over in January 1966 and was killed in July of that year.

questions.question: In which year did the Second Republic begin under President Shehu Shagari?
questions.explanation: Civilian rule returned on 1 October 1979.

questions.question: Who overthrew the Shagari government on 31 December 1983?
questions.explanation: Major General Muhammadu Buhari led the coup that ended the Second Republic.

questions.question: In which year was Head of State Murtala Mohammed assassinated?
questions.explanation: He was killed on 13 February 1976 during a failed coup attempt.

questions.question: Who handed power back to civilians in 1979 after succeeding Murtala Mohammed?
questions.explanation: Obasanjo led the military government from 1976 and handed over to Shehu Shagari in 1979.

questions.question: Which city hosted FESTAC '77, the Second World Black and African Festival of Arts and Culture?
questions.explanation: The festival was held in Lagos in January and February 1977.

questions.question: Who became the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1986?
questions.explanation: Wole Soyinka received the 1986 prize.

questions.question: Which region was created in 1963 out of part of the Western Region?
questions.explanation: The Mid-Western Region was created in August 1963.

questions.question: How many states did General Gowon create in May 1967?
questions.explanation: Gowon created 12 states from the four existing regions.

questions.question: In which year did Nigeria's number of states reach 36?
questions.explanation: Six more states were created in October 1996, bringing the total to 36.

questions.question: Who was the first Nigerian Governor-General of the Federation, from 1960 to 1963?
questions.explanation: Nnamdi Azikiwe held the office before it became the presidency in 1963.

questions.question: Who became the first woman and the first African to lead the World Trade Organization, in 2021?
questions.explanation: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala took office as WTO Director-General in March 2021.

questions.question: When did the Nigerian Civil War end?
questions.explanation: Biafran forces surrendered in January 1970.

questions.question: What were the '3Rs' announced by the government after the civil war?
questions.explanation: The 3Rs were Reconciliation, Rehabilitation and Reconstruction.

questions.question: In which year were permanent voter cards and card readers used in a general election for the first time?
questions.explanation: Card readers were deployed nationwide in the 2015 general elections.

questions.question: Which city was the capital of the former Northern Region?
questions.explanation: Kaduna was the regional capital.

questions.question: Nigeria takes its name from which river?
questions.explanation: The name 'Nigeria' comes from the River Niger.

questions.question: Who led the jihad that founded the Sokoto Caliphate in the early 1800s?
questions.explanation: Usman dan Fodio led the movement that founded the caliphate around 1804.

questions.question: Which historic kingdom was famous for its bronze plaques, many of which were taken by British forces in 1897?
questions.explanation: The Kingdom of Benin's bronzes were taken after the British expedition of 1897.

questions.question: In which year did the naira replace the Nigerian pound?
questions.explanation: The naira and kobo were introduced in January 1973.
